title: The Element We Found in the Sun First — Helium, 1868
description:
In 1868 a bright yellow line appeared in the Sun's spectrum during a total eclipse — at a wavelength no known element on Earth could produce. It took twenty-seven years, a rock from Norway and one chemist who doubted a colleague's paperwork before anyone held the gas in a bottle.

This is the story of helium: the only element first discovered somewhere other than this planet.

PRIMARY SOURCES
- P. J. C. Janssen, communication read to the Académie des Sciences, 26 October 1868 (observation at Guntur, 18 August 1868).
- J. N. Lockyer and E. Frankland on the chromospheric line D3, 1868–1869.
- W. F. Hillebrand, "On the Occurrence of Nitrogen in Uraninite", Bulletin of the U.S. Geological Survey 78 (1890).
- W. Ramsay, isolation of helium from cleveite, 26 March 1895; samples confirmed spectroscopically by W. Crookes and J. N. Lockyer.
- P. T. Cleve and N. A. Langlet, helium in cleveite and its atomic weight, 1895.
- H. Kamerlingh Onnes, liquefaction of helium, Leiden, 1908.
- U.S. Bureau of Land Management, Federal Helium Reserve at Amarillo; the remaining reserve was sold to the Messer Group in June 2024.
